intro.back: 10 questions about Lessons 10–14. Take your time. You can look at the lessons again and try again as often as you want.
intro.source: 10 questions about Lessons 10–14. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.0.question.back: In olden times, why did towns often grow in places where boats stopped on a river?
questions.0.question.source: Long ago, why did towns often grow at places where boats stopped on a river?

questions.0.options.0.text.back: Boats stopped the river from flooding
questions.0.options.0.text.source: Boats kept the river from flooding

questions.0.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite yet. Boats cannot stop a river from flooding. Towns grew where boats stopped because people could trade there. Look at Lesson 10 again.
questions.0.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Boats cannot stop a river from flooding. Towns grew where boats stopped because people could trade there. Look back at Lesson 10.

questions.0.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. Boats carry heavy goods, such as grain and wood. People buy and sell these goods at the places where boats stop.
questions.0.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Boats carried heavy goods, like grain and wood. People bought and sold these goods where the boats stopped.

questions.0.options.2.text.back: The land is high and rocky
questions.0.options.2.text.source: The land was high and rocky

questions.0.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite yet. Boats stop at the water's edge, not on high, rocky land. Look at Lesson 10 again.
questions.0.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Boats stop by the water, not on high, rocky land. Look back at Lesson 10.

questions.1.stimulus.title.back: Notes from the made-up map of Riverlands in Lesson 10
questions.1.stimulus.title.source: Notes from the made-up Riverlands map in Lesson 10

questions.1.stimulus.items.0.note: Translator: 'River site / Hill site / Forest site' are rendered as 'Kawasan Sungai / Kawasan Bukit / Kawasan Hutan'. They must match the names used in the Malay Lesson 10 map. 'Tanah' is used for both 'land' and 'soil' because 'tanih' may be too technical for young readers. Please check this reads clearly. Back-translation check: The translator's flag still stands. 'Kawasan Sungai / Kawasan Bukit / Kawasan Hutan' must match the site names on the Malay Lesson 10 map. 'Tanah' is used for both 'land' and 'soil' ('tanih' may be too technical). Check this reads clearly.
questions.1.stimulus.items.0.back: River Area: flat land at the edge of the river. The soil is good for crops. Sometimes the river floods it.
questions.1.stimulus.items.0.source: River site: flat land by the river. The soil is good for crops. Sometimes the river floods it.

questions.1.stimulus.items.1.back: Hill Area: high, dry land. Floods do not reach there. The soil is thin and rocky.
questions.1.stimulus.items.1.source: Hill site: high, dry ground. Floods do not reach it. The soil is thin and rocky.

questions.1.stimulus.items.2.back: Forest Area: far from the river. There is wood for building. People must cut down trees before farming.
questions.1.stimulus.items.2.source: Forest site: far from the river. There is wood to build with. People must cut trees before they farm.

questions.1.question.back: Which fact is a good reason to build a farming town in the River Area?
questions.1.question.source: Which fact is a good reason to build a farming town at the River site?

questions.1.options.0.text.back: The soil there is good for crops.
questions.1.options.0.text.source: The soil there is good for crops.

questions.1.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. The map states that the soil in the River Area is good for crops. Mud from the river makes the soil fertile.
questions.1.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The map says the soil at the River site is good for crops. Mud from the river makes the land fertile.

questions.1.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite yet. Floods do not reach the Hill Area. But the river sometimes floods the River Area. Look at Lesson 10 again.
questions.1.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Floods do not reach the Hill site. But the river sometimes floods the River site. Look back at Lesson 10.

questions.1.options.2.text.back: There is wood for building there.
questions.1.options.2.text.source: There is wood to build with there.

questions.1.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite yet. The wood is in the Forest Area. The River Area is flat land next to the river. Look at Lesson 10 again.
questions.1.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The wood is at the Forest site. The River site is flat land next to the river. Look back at Lesson 10.

questions.2.question.back: Which part of a map tells you what each colour, line and shape means?
questions.2.question.source: Which part of a map tells you what each colour, line and shape means?

questions.2.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite yet. The scale helps you see the real distance between places. Look at Lesson 11 again.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The scale helps you see how far things are in real life. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.2.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite yet. The compass points show the directions north, south, east and west. Look at Lesson 11 again.
questions.2.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The compass rose shows north, south, east and west. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.2.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. The key, or legend, tells you what each symbol means. For example, a blue line can stand for a river.
questions.2.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. The key, or legend, tells you what each symbol means. For example, a blue line can stand for a river.

questions.3.stimulus.title.note: Translator: 'Ambrey Park' is kept as a name, following the brief. 'Taman Ambrey' would sound more natural in Malaysia. Please decide. Back-translation check: The translator's flag still stands. 'Ambrey Park' is kept as a name, as the brief says. 'Taman Ambrey' would sound more natural in Malaysia. Decide which to use, and use it the same way in Lesson 11.
questions.3.stimulus.title.source: A made-up map of Ambrey Park

questions.3.stimulus.items.1.back: The length of the path from the gate to the pond is five squares.
questions.3.stimulus.items.1.source: The path from the gate to the pond is five squares long.

questions.3.stimulus.items.2.back: Compass points: N (north) points to the top of the map
questions.3.stimulus.items.2.source: Compass rose: N (north) points to the top of the map

questions.3.question.back: About how long is the path from the gate to the pond?
questions.3.question.source: About how long is the path from the gate to the pond?

questions.3.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite yet. The path is five squares long, and each square is 10 metres. Look at Lesson 11 again.
questions.3.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The path is five squares long, and each square is 10 metres. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.3.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. Each square is 10 metres. Five squares make 50 metres.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Each square is 10 metres. Five squares make 50 metres.

questions.3.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite yet. That is the same as 50 squares. The path is only five squares, each one 10 metres. Look at Lesson 11 again.
questions.3.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. That would be 50 squares. The path is only five squares of 10 metres each. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.4.question.back: Nairobi and Shenzhen are two real cities. What helped both of them grow?
questions.4.question.source: Nairobi and Shenzhen are two real cities. What helped both of them grow?

questions.4.options.0.text.back: Cool weather and lots of rain
questions.4.options.0.text.source: Cool weather and lots of rain

questions.4.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite yet. Weather did not make these two cities grow. Nairobi began as a stopping place on a railway line, and Shenzhen grew when factories opened. Look at Lesson 12 again.
questions.4.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Weather did not make these two cities grow. Nairobi began as a stop on a railway, and Shenzhen grew when factories opened. Look back at Lesson 12.

questions.4.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite yet. Fertile soil helps farms produce crops. These two cities grew because of jobs and transport. Look at Lesson 12 again.
questions.4.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Rich soil helps farms grow crops. These two cities grew because of jobs and transport. Look back at Lesson 12.

questions.4.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. Nairobi began as a stopping place on a railway line, and factories opened in Shenzhen. Jobs and transport brought many people there.
questions.4.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Nairobi began as a stop on a railway, and factories opened in Shenzhen. Jobs and transport brought many people.

questions.5.stimulus.body.back: A new railway line opens in the made-up town of Ostrin. A factory opens next to the station, with 600 new jobs. Five years later, the number of people in Ostrin has doubled. But the town still has only one small school.
questions.5.stimulus.body.source: A new train line opens in the made-up town of Ostrin. A factory opens next to the station, with 600 new jobs. Five years later, twice as many people live in Ostrin. But the town still has only one small school.

questions.5.question.back: What problem is Ostrin most likely to face?
questions.5.question.source: What problem is Ostrin most likely to have?

questions.5.options.0.text.back: The only school becomes very crowded.
questions.5.options.0.text.source: The one school gets very crowded.

questions.5.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. The number of people grew quickly, but the school did not. A service needs to grow when the number of people grows.
questions.5.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The number of people grew fast, but the school did not. A service needs to grow when the population grows.

questions.5.options.1.text.back: Jobs in the town are getting fewer.
questions.5.options.1.text.source: There are fewer jobs in the town.

questions.5.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite yet. The factory brought 600 new jobs, so jobs increased, not decreased. Look at Lesson 12 again.
questions.5.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The factory brought 600 new jobs, so there are more jobs, not fewer. Look back at Lesson 12.

questions.5.options.2.text.back: It is hard to go to other towns.
questions.5.options.2.text.source: It is hard to get to other towns.

questions.5.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite yet. The new railway line makes travel easier. Think about the school instead. Look at Lesson 12 again.
questions.5.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The new train line makes travel easier. Think about the school instead. Look back at Lesson 12.

questions.6.stimulus.body.back: Kelmar is a made-up town. For the past 40 years, its summers have been hot and dry. Most of its rain falls in winter. Today, a cold wind is blowing, and grey clouds cover the sky.
questions.6.stimulus.body.source: Kelmar is a made-up town. For the last 40 years, its summers have been hot and dry. Most of its rain has fallen in winter. Today, a cool wind is blowing, and grey clouds cover the sky.

questions.6.question.back: Which one is about weather, not climate?
questions.6.question.source: Which one is about weather, not climate?

questions.6.options.0.text.back: Summers are usually hot and dry.
questions.6.options.0.text.source: Summers are usually hot and dry.

questions.6.options.0.feedback.note: Back-translation check: 'Keadaan udara' is a close match for the English 'what the air is like now'. A Malaysian child might read it as air quality, though. Match the weather definition in the Malay Lesson 13. 'Keadaan cuaca/atmosfera' is an option, but it is more circular or technical.
questions.6.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite yet. This is a pattern over many years, so this is climate. Weather is the condition of the air right now. Look at Lesson 13 again.
questions.6.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. This is a pattern over many years, so it is climate. Weather is what the air is like now. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.6.options.1.text.back: A cold wind is blowing today.
questions.6.options.1.text.source: A cool wind is blowing today.

questions.6.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. This is about one day only, and it can change quickly. That is why this is weather.
questions.6.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. This is about one day, and it can change fast. That makes it weather.

questions.6.options.2.feedback.note: Back-translation check: Same 'keadaan udara' question as in questions.6.options.0.feedback. Keep both rows the same as the Malay Lesson 13.
questions.6.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite yet. This is something that usually happens every year, so this is climate. Weather is the condition of the air right now. Look at Lesson 13 again.
questions.6.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. This is what usually happens each year, so it is climate. Weather is what the air is like now. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.7.question.back: What are the seasons like in areas near the equator?
questions.7.question.source: What are the seasons like near the equator?

questions.7.options.0.text.note: Translator: To keep the option short, this lists 'Musim bunga, panas, luruh dan sejuk' without repeating 'musim' each time. Check this reads naturally.

questions.7.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite yet. Many places far from the equator have these four seasons. Look at Lesson 13 again.
questions.7.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Many places far from the equator have these four seasons. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.7.options.1.text.back: Cold and snowy all year round

questions.7.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite yet. Places near the equator are hot all year round. Look at Lesson 13 again.
questions.7.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Places near the equator are warm all year. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.7.options.2.text.back: A rainy season and a dry season
questions.7.options.2.text.source: A rainy season and a dry season

questions.7.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. Near the equator, the weather is hot all year round. So the seasons are usually a rainy season or a dry season.
questions.7.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Near the equator, it is warm all year. So the seasons are usually rainy or dry.

questions.8.stimulus.title.note: Back-translation check: Changed 'dari Pelajaran 14' to 'dalam Pelajaran 14'. 'Dari' is for places and times. 'Dalam' also matches Question 2 ('dalam Pelajaran 10').
questions.8.stimulus.title.back: The made-up town of Brookside from Lesson 14: three ideas for the low bridge
questions.8.stimulus.title.source: The made-up town of Brookside from Lesson 14: three ideas for a low bridge

questions.8.stimulus.items.0.note: Translator: 'Covers with water' is rendered as 'menenggelamkan' (submerges). Please check this is not too strong. Back-translation check: Rewrote this line because 'menenggelamkan' (submerge/sink) could sound like the bridge itself sinks. The new line says 'when there is heavy rain, water sometimes covers the low footbridge'. Have a native speaker check it, and match the wording in Lesson 14.
questions.8.stimulus.items.0.back: The problem: heavy rain sometimes submerges the low footbridge.
questions.8.stimulus.items.0.source: The problem: heavy rain sometimes covers the low footbridge with water.

questions.8.stimulus.items.1.back: Idea A: put up warning signs at the side of the bridge. It is cheap and quick.
questions.8.stimulus.items.1.source: Idea A: put a warning sign by the bridge. It is cheap and quick.

questions.8.stimulus.items.2.note: Translator: 'Ramp' is rendered as 'landaian'. Check whether 'ram' or 'laluan landai' is more familiar, and match Lesson 14. Back-translation check: The translator's flag still stands. 'Landaian' (ramp): check it against Lesson 14, and check whether 'laluan landai' or 'ram' is more familiar. Don't use 'tanjakan', which the back-translator mentioned: it is more Indonesian.
questions.8.stimulus.items.2.back: Idea B: build the bridge higher and add ramps. It costs more and takes months.
questions.8.stimulus.items.2.source: Idea B: build the bridge higher and add a ramp. It costs more and takes months.

questions.8.stimulus.items.3.back: Idea C: send phone messages and stick up paper notices when heavy rain is going to fall.
questions.8.stimulus.items.3.source: Idea C: send phone messages and put up paper notices when heavy rain is coming.

questions.8.question.back: What is one problem with Idea A, that is, the warning signs?
questions.8.question.source: What is one problem with Idea A, the warning sign?

questions.8.options.0.text.back: It does not make the bridge safer.
questions.8.options.0.text.source: It does not make the bridge safer.

questions.8.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. Signs are quick and cheap, but the bridge stays low. Also, some people cannot read the signs.
questions.8.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. A sign is quick and cheap, but the bridge stays low. Also, some people cannot read the sign.

questions.8.options.1.text.back: It costs a lot and takes months.
questions.8.options.1.text.source: It costs a lot and takes months.

questions.8.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite yet. That is Idea B, that is, raising the bridge. Signs are cheap and quick. Look at Lesson 14 again.
questions.8.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. That is Idea B, raising the bridge. A sign is cheap and quick. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.8.options.2.text.note: Back-translation check: Changed 'perlu telefon' to 'memerlukan telefon'. 'Perlu telefon' could be read as 'need to phone (someone)'.
questions.8.options.2.text.back: Everyone needs a phone to see them.
questions.8.options.2.text.source: Everyone needs a phone to see it.

questions.8.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite yet. Phone messages are part of Idea C. The signs stand at the side of the bridge, so no phone is needed. Look at Lesson 14 again.
questions.8.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Phone messages are part of Idea C. A sign stands by the bridge, so no phone is needed. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.9.question.back: A made-up library puts its signs in three languages and adds pictures. Now everyone can find what they need. This is an example of what?
questions.9.question.source: A made-up library puts its signs in three languages and adds pictures. Now everyone can find what they need. What is this an example of?

questions.9.options.0.text.note: Translator: 'Alert' is rendered as 'amaran' (warning). Match the Lesson 14 glossary. Back-translation check: The translator's flag still stands. 'Alert' is translated as 'amaran' (warning). It must match the Lesson 14 glossary term, and the feedback for option A must use the same word.

questions.9.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite yet. A warning is a message that tells people about danger. These signs help people find things. Look at Lesson 14 again.
questions.9.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. An alert is a message that warns people about danger. These signs help people find things. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.9.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite yet. The environment is the land, water, air, plants and animals around us. Look at Lesson 14 again.
questions.9.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The environment is the land, water, air, plants and animals around us. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.9.options.2.text.note: Translator: 'Inclusion' is rendered as 'keterangkuman'. 'Inklusiviti' or 'sifat inklusif' are also used in Malaysia. Match the glossary term in Lesson 14. Back-translation check: The translator's flag still stands. 'Keterangkuman' is formal and many 10–17-year-olds may not know it. It must match the Lesson 14 glossary term ('inklusiviti' and 'sifat inklusif' are other options). If it changes, update the feedback for option C too.

questions.9.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. Inclusion means making sure everyone can take part. Signs in three languages, with pictures, help more people.
questions.9.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Inclusion means making sure everyone can take part. Signs in three languages, with pictures, help more people.
